bear_case: G32 has a user but no buyer. Installation and base spectrum managers are compliance and records staff inside a NEC or communications squadron (DAFI 17-221; CJCSM 3320.02E) whose purchasing authority is a handheld analyzer, not a whole-base sensor network or a new workflow system; range frequency offices sit inside range infrastructure vehicles held by primes (e.g., the Space Force $981M test/training IDIQ, 2026-07-31). The money that does exist for the problem was committed in 2026 to already-selected vendors: OUSW(R&E)'s $100M-ceiling OTA to Hidden Level for passive sensing over bases, ranges and border (2026-07-30), the Army's $350M-ceiling S2AS production to 3dB Labs whose stated scope includes EMI resolution and warning of unauthorized interference sources (2026-06-01), and ~$196M of REWSI spectrum-sensor production (Aug-Sep 2026). The ticket and assignment workflow is government-owned by DISA DSO - Spectrum XXI is the mandated tool, JSIRO is the ticket system, a SOSC helpdesk contract runs to Sept 2026 and the EMBM-J SA recompete is in flight - so an offline client has a single captive buyer that can order offline modes from contractors it already pays. On the civil side, CBRS interference is resolved by SAS administrators, shared-band measurement is done by NIST/ITS/NASA/MITRE under NASCTN (NIST, Sept 2026), and Aurora Insight is the precedent for a standalone spectrum-data business failing to scale. No SBIR/STTR, DIU, AFWERX or CSO topic for this scope surfaced (this session; corpus E04-F31). The result is consultancy drift: the only revenue shapes are pilots, CRADAs and licensed modules.
strongest_single_argument: The PROBLEM -> USER chain ends at the user: no requirement owner, program office, budget line or vehicle exists for third-party installation interference-geolocation software or an offline spectrum client, and every adjacent funded buyer (Hidden Level OTA, S2AS, REWSI, DISA DSO tools) is already committed to another vendor as of Sept 2026.

what_would_change_my_mind: An IMCOM/AFIMSC/NETCOM or DISA DSO sources-sought, CSO or OTA explicitly for installation-level interference geolocation or a disconnected JSIR/assignment client; an R-1/P-1 line or PE number funding it; or two signed paid pilots from installations or CBRS operators at more than $50k each proving a buyer with signature authority exists.
narrower_survivable_version: A subcontract/licensing business: supply the TDOA/AoA fusion module to a sensor OEM or the EMBM-J/EWPMT-X integrator, or build the offline JSIR client under a CRADA and sell sustainment - a small services company, not a venture.

bear_case: The gap assumes the geolocation software is the missing piece, but it is the most commoditized piece. Rohde & Schwarz publishes a hybrid AOA/TDOA white paper and sells modular, scalable systems; Keysight's KSMS runs TDoA on three synchronized FieldFox handhelds an installation may already own; CRFS RFeye arrays do AoA, TDoA and PoA; and a 2026 NAVIGATION paper shows jammer/spoofer localization on a low-cost SDR array, so the algorithms are public. At the bottom of the market KrakenRF ships RDF Pro multi-station fusion with a ~EUR 1,063 node and Wavelet Lab already sells a multi-node SDR TDOA/FDOA geolocation platform - the exact 'software on commodity SDR' proposition. In the middle, Distributed Spectrum has raised ~$29M (Series A Mar 2025, Conviction/Shield Capital), positions on commodity hardware plus algorithms, held an AFRL SBIR Phase II for low-SWaP RF SA and an SBIR to improve transmitter localization on its low-cost SDR network, and holds DoD relationships a student team lacks. Hidden Level holds the base/range OTA and can license its processing onto cheaper nodes. For the workflow client, DISA's contractors (the GEMSIS sustainment vendor; Palantir for EMBM-J DS) and the Army's EWPMT-X integrator own the systems of record and their non-public APIs; an offline JRFL/JSIR mode is a capability drop for them, and the government prefers to own TAK components. Switching cost for a spectrum manager is nil because the startup would import/export the same SFAF/JSIR files as everyone else. Anduril, Palantir and L3Harris do not need to add it; smaller, already-funded vendors already have.
strongest_single_argument: Every price tier of the proposed product already has a seller - R&S/CRFS/Keysight at the top, Distributed Spectrum ($29M, DoD SBIRs on localization) and Hidden Level ($100M OTA) in the funded middle, Wavelet Lab and KrakenSDR RDF Pro at the bottom - and the workflow client's systems of record (Spectrum XXI, JSIRO, EMBM-J, EWPMT-X) are owned by DISA/PM EW&C contractors who can add offline modes on request.

what_would_change_my_mind: Independent (non-vendor) test data showing the founders' engine beats Distributed Spectrum, Wavelet Lab and a KrakenSDR RDF Pro baseline on CEP and false-fix rate per dollar in a dense installation environment; or evidence that DISA DSO or PM EW&C intends to compete an offline spectrum-management client rather than assign it to incumbents.
narrower_survivable_version: Do not sell a product; license the calibration/false-fix engine as a module to one of the funded sensor vendors, or contribute the offline JSIR/SFAF client as an open ATAK-CIV plugin and sell integration services around it.

bear_case: This is the one form in the G21/G11 family the team can actually build: no hardware to manufacture, commodity SDRs at ~EUR 1,000 per node, published algorithms, an unclassified MVP under $120k, and a product that - if scoped to civil receive-only monitoring without military DF/EW features - is plausibly EAR rather than ITAR so the Indonesian founder can work on the core (counsel must confirm; E07-F16/F17). Feasibility therefore does not kill it. Access does. A demo that an installation or DISA JSC would credit needs a real base site, real SFAF assignments and real JSIR records, all CUI (JRFL possibly classified), obtainable only through a sponsor the founders do not have and handled only by U.S.-person staff under DFARS 7012/NIST 800-171 - so the non-U.S.-person co-founder is excluded from exactly the data that makes the product real (E07-F30). SBIR/STTR, the natural $150k-$1.5M bridge, is closed unless the cap table is restructured (13 CFR 121.702). The founders' first customers are therefore civil pilots and OEM licenses, both of which cap the company at a small business; a five-year procurement cycle is not the issue because there is no procurement to wait for. The MVP is under $100k, but the credible-demo stage ($0.5-1.5M) requires the sponsor relationship and U.S.-person hires the team lacks.
strongest_single_argument: The team can build and legally demonstrate the civil-scoped engine for under $120k, but the data and site access that would make it credible to a military buyer are CUI held by sponsors the founders cannot reach and cannot share with the non-U.S.-person co-founder, and the SBIR bridge is closed by ownership - so feasibility confirms a small-business path and refutes a venture path.

what_would_change_my_mind: A signed CRADA or paid pilot with a named installation, range or DISA JSC that supplies sanitized assignment/JSIR data; a counsel opinion confirming EAR jurisdiction for the DF-capable product; or a cap-table restructure and a U.S.-person technical lead that reopens SBIR/STTR.
narrower_survivable_version: An EAR-scoped civil interference-geolocation SaaS for private-5G/CBRS operators, ranges and venues, built and sold by the founders with the Indonesian founder on the core code, with defense entry deferred to a licensed-module or CRADA role once a sponsor supplies data - a founder-accessible small business.
